Build bilateral interactive surface reports

Bradley Buchsbaum

2026-11-12

Source: vignettes/interactive-surfaces.Rmd
interactive-surfaces.Rmd

An HTML report often needs one interactive figure for both hemispheres and several result maps. Repeating a widget for every map wastes space and sends the same mesh to the browser many times. surface_scene() describes the geometries, maps, labels, and fallback once; surfwidget() displays that scene in R Markdown or Quarto; and write_surface_scene() writes the same scene as an ordinary web page.

This article builds one bilateral viewer with two selectable maps. The example uses package data, runs without a network connection, and keeps the scientific transformation in R.

What does a scene contain?

A SurfaceScene has one SurfaceGeometry per hemisphere and one or more named scalar layers. Each bilateral layer supplies a left and right value vector whose lengths match the corresponding geometry. A scene also records the initial map, legend metadata, provenance, alternative text, and fallback text.

The example uses the fsaverage5 template bundled with neurosurf: inflated surfaces for display, white surfaces to place the example clusters, sulcal depth for the grey anatomy underneath the maps, and the cortex mask that keeps colour off the medial wall in the static figure.

inflated <- load_fsaverage("fsaverage5", "inflated")
white <- load_fsaverage("fsaverage5", "white")
sulc <- load_fsaverage_sulc("fsaverage5")
cortex <- load_fsaverage_cortex("fsaverage5")

# Display anatomy, lighter on gyri. FreeSurfer sulc is positive in
# sulci, so it is negated. The report preset's grey ramp saturates at
# |0.1|; scaling to that range keeps it continuous and quiet.
anatomy <- list(
  left = 0.2 * normalize_surface_anatomy(-sulc$lh, "continuous"),
  right = 0.2 * normalize_surface_anatomy(-sulc$rh, "continuous")
)

The browser renders the values that R supplies. Perform thresholding, capping, atlas projection, and other scientific transformations before constructing a layer. Here two synthetic z maps are built from smooth clusters placed at white-surface coordinates and falling off with distance over the inflated surface:

cluster <- function(hemi, centre, peak, width = 12) {
  seed <- which.min(colSums((t(coords(white[[hemi]])) - centre)^2))
  xyz <- coords(inflated[[hemi]])
  peak * exp(-colSums((t(xyz) - xyz[seed, ])^2) / (2 * width^2))
}
contrast <- function(centres, lh_peaks, rh_peaks) {
  one_side <- function(hemi, side, peaks) {
    Reduce(`+`, Map(function(centre, peak) {
      cluster(hemi, centre * c(side, 1, 1), peak)
    }, centres, peaks))
  }
  list(left = one_side("lh", -1, lh_peaks),
       right = one_side("rh", 1, rh_peaks))
}

memory <- contrast(
  centres = list(c(45, -60, 20), c(40, 20, 30), c(55, -20, 0)),
  lh_peaks = c(4, 3, -3.5), rh_peaks = c(3.5, 2.5, -2.8)
)
# A right-hand movement: left motor cortex dominates
motor <- contrast(
  centres = list(c(38, -22, 56), c(10, -60, 50)),
  lh_peaks = c(4.5, -3), rh_peaks = c(-2.2, -3)
)

A binary region of interest, used below as a reference layer: every vertex within 18 mm of a point in the intraparietal sulcus, again measured over the inflated surface.

roi <- function(hemi, centre, radius = 18) {
  seed <- which.min(colSums((t(coords(white[[hemi]])) - centre)^2))
  xyz <- coords(inflated[[hemi]])
  as.numeric(colSums((t(xyz) - xyz[seed, ])^2) < radius^2)
}
region <- list(left = roi("lh", c(-30, -55, 45)),
               right = roi("rh", c(30, -55, 45)))

How do you build one bilateral, multi-map viewer?

Create each named map with surface_layer(), then put both geometries and all layers in one scene. selected_layer chooses the map shown when the viewer opens.

For thresholded two-sided maps, use a palette whose tails start at clearly visible colours and never pass through the light anatomy grey: blue for negative, red for positive. surface_palette() with the same limits and threshold returns exactly the colours surface_figure() would use, so the interactive and static figures agree. The layer’s threshold hides |z| < 2 and marks the gap in the colour key; magnitude_opacity fades colour in between |z| = 2 and 2.6, so cluster edges are smooth instead of following the mesh’s triangles. Unthresholded values are passed in, and NA is kept for genuinely missing data.

z_colors <- surface_palette("two_sided", limits = c(-5, 5),
                            threshold = 2)
z_layer <- function(name, values, title) {
  surface_layer(name, values, colormap = z_colors, limits = c(-5, 5),
                threshold = c(-2, 2), units = "z",
                magnitude_opacity = list(low = 2, high = 2.6),
                legend = list(title = title))
}

scene <- surface_scene(
  left = inflated$lh,
  right = inflated$rh,
  curvature = anatomy,
  layers = list(
    z_layer("memory", memory, "Memory contrast"),
    z_layer("motor", motor, "Motor contrast")
  ),
  selected_layer = "memory",
  metadata = list(template = "fsaverage5"),
  provenance = list(source = "synthetic clusters on package data"),
  fallback = "Inflated cortical surfaces with two thresholded z maps.",
  alt_text = paste(
    "Inflated left and right cortical surfaces showing a selectable",
    "thresholded z map, blue negative and red positive, |z| above 2."
  ),
  preset = "report",
  mode = "report"
)

Pass the scene to surfwidget() once. The map selector changes the active values and legend without constructing another widget or another WebGL context.

surfwidget(scene, width = "100%", height = "420px")

The report toolbar provides the authored map selector, coordinated anatomical views, reset, and PNG export. Drag to rotate, use the wheel or a pinch gesture to zoom, and right-drag to pan.

How do you keep a reference region beneath the selected effect map?

Give one binary layer role = "reference" and an explicit color. It has its own checkbox, opacity slider and categorical swatch. It stays beneath either quantitative map and cannot become the selected map or enter effect readouts. Reset restores its authored visibility and opacity.

reference_scene <- surface_scene(
  left = inflated$lh, right = inflated$rh,
  layers = c(scene@layers, list(surface_layer(
    "reference", region, role = "reference", color = "#238b45",
    opacity = 0.4, legend = list(title = "Intraparietal ROI"),
    provenance = list(source = "synthetic 18 mm disc")
  ))),
  curvature = anatomy,
  preset = "report",
  fallback = "Bilateral z maps over a faint intraparietal ROI.",
  alt_text = "Thresholded z maps over a green intraparietal region."
)
stopifnot(identical(reference_scene@selected_layer, "memory"))
surfwidget(reference_scene, width = "100%", height = "360px")

In the viewer the green region sits beneath whichever map is selected and keeps its own swatch, checkbox and opacity slider; it never enters the colour key. (The widget is not embedded here to keep this article small; the static figure below shows the same composition.) References require a full 0/1 mask per hemisphere, with no limits, units, indices or thresholds.

The CPU renderer draws the same membership beneath a static map, in the order anatomy, reference, effect:

image <- render_surface_rgba(
  inflated$lh, memory$left, anatomy_metric = sulc$lh,
  cortex_mask = cortex$lh,
  threshold = 2, limits = c(-5, 5), alpha_ramp = 0.6,
  reference = list(
    id = "reference", label = "Intraparietal ROI",
    mask = region$left, color = "#238b45", opacity = 0.4
  ),
  width = 680, height = 420, antialias = 2
)
surface_panels(image, labels = NULL, legend_title = "z",
               references = c("Intraparietal ROI" = "#238b45"))

Left hemisphere, lateral view: the intraparietal ROI (green, 40% opacity) beneath the memory z map.

Both renderers classify membership at 0.5 after linear interpolation, and when a cortex mask is supplied, triangles outside it never receive reference colour. A static figure should label the reference with its own swatch, outside the effect colour scale, as surface_panels() does above.

Supply already projected binary membership. For a volume label, use explicit categorical/nearest-voxel sampling and record the source and mesh identity, depth aggregation and projection parameters in provenance. This API does not perform projection or inference.

Which option controls appearance and behavior?

preset sets appearance and mode sets behaviour; the scene above uses preset = "report" with mode = "report".

Setting Controls What it changes
preset = "report" Appearance Quiet sulcal greys on a neutral grey panel, lit for on-screen reading; made for report widgets. Its grey ramp turns two-tone unless the anatomy is scaled, as above.
preset = "paper-light" Appearance White background, stronger folding contrast, and print-oriented PNG defaults.
mode = "report" Behavior Lazy mounting, the compact report toolbar, deterministic initial framing, and fallback/print behavior.
mode = "viewer" Behavior A bare rotatable viewer without the report toolbar.

Tweakpane is deprecated. The report runtime does not load it or contact a CDN. Legacy showControls and controlType configuration entries warn during the migration; use the scene mode instead.

How is geometry shared across maps?

surface_scene_manifest() converts numeric arrays to typed binary assets and addresses each asset by its SHA-256 digest. The scene refers to each hemisphere geometry once. Each additional full bilateral map contributes two value arrays, not another copy of the vertices or faces.

manifest <- surface_scene_manifest(scene, asset_mode = "inline")
roles <- vapply(manifest$assets, `[[`, character(1), "role")
bytes <- vapply(manifest$assets, `[[`, numeric(1), "byteLength")

data.frame(
  content = c("geometry", "map values"),
  assets = c(sum(roles %in% c("vertices", "faces", "curvature")),
             sum(roles == "values")),
  bytes = c(sum(bytes[roles %in% c("vertices", "faces", "curvature")]),
            sum(bytes[roles == "values"]))
)
#>      content assets  bytes
#> 1   geometry      5 573504
#> 2 map values      4 163872

Missing map values remain IEEE NaN values in the binary payload. The browser verifies every adjacent asset’s byte length and checksum before constructing the scene.

How do you write an offline report?

Use write_surface_scene() when the viewer must live outside an R Markdown or Quarto document. Both output modes bundle the compatible surfviewjs runtime locally and make no network requests.

# index.html, the runtime, and content-addressed .bin files
write_surface_scene(scene, "surface-report", self_contained = FALSE)

# one index.html with the runtime and typed arrays inlined
write_surface_scene(scene, "surface-report-inline",
                    self_contained = TRUE)

Choose adjacent assets for a site or a report directory: the browser can cache the runtime and SHA-addressed arrays, and repeated assets are deduplicated. Choose a self-contained file when a single portable HTML file matters more than file size or cross-page caching.

How do you mount the scene on a plain web page?

The HTML writer produces a minimal page that uses the public surfview.mountSurfView() API. You can customize its generated index.html or use the same lifecycle in another page. In this example, manifest is a surfview.scene.v1 object produced by surface_scene_manifest():

<div id="surface-report"></div>
<script src="./surfview.embed.iife.js"></script>
<script>
  const handle = surfview.mountSurfView(
    document.getElementById("surface-report"),
    manifest,
    {
      lazy: true,
      preset: "paper-light",
      controls: true,
      baseUrl: document.baseURI,
      bilateralGroup: {
        id: "bilateral",
        leftSurfaceId: "left",
        rightSurfaceId: "right"
      }
    }
  );

  handle.ready.then(() => handle.setView("lateral"));
  window.addEventListener("pagehide", () => handle.dispose(),
                          { once: true });
</script>

A manifest with both hemispheres must name a bilateralGroup that pairs the left and right surface ids; without it the report runtime refuses to mount. surfwidget() and write_surface_scene() supply this option automatically.

The returned handle also provides selectLayer(), resize(), exportPNG(), and dispose(). Call dispose() when an application removes or replaces the viewer so it can release observers, listeners, animation frames, the WebGL context, and GPU resources.

What happens when interaction is unavailable?

fallback is required plain text. The widget and standalone writer expose it when JavaScript is disabled or WebGL initialization fails, and print CSS shows it instead of a blank canvas. alt_text labels the interactive figure for assistive technology.

The fallback text is not a bitmap renderer. If a report needs a visual print, PDF, or archival representation, build a static figure from the same R values with surface_figure(); see vignette("surface-figures").

When should you use the legacy shortcuts?

surfwidget() still accepts SurfaceGeometry, NeuroSurface, ColorMappedNeuroSurface, and VertexColoredNeuroSurface. Those methods adapt a single surface to a SurfaceScene and are useful for quick exploration:

surface <- NeuroSurface(inflated$lh, nodes(inflated$lh), memory$left)
surfwidget(surface, irange = c(-5, 5))

Use an explicit SurfaceScene for bilateral figures, multiple named maps, portable assets, authored fallback text, provenance, or report behavior.
